items.title: Share a subnet with AWS RAM and read the permission it uses
items.kills: "Sharing a resource with AWS RAM copies the resource into the other account."
items.cost: $0: a VPC, a subnet and a resource share have no charge of their own.
items.cost_if_forgotten: $0 a day. Delete them anyway, so that no unused share stays in the account.
items.read_only_alternative: These commands change nothing. List the managed permissions for subnets: aws ram list-permissions --resource-type ec2:Subnet --query "permissions[].[name,isResourceTypeDefault]" Then read the actions of the default one: aws ram get-permission --permission-arn arn:aws:ram::aws:permission/AWSRAMDefaultPermissionSubnet --query "permission.permission" Expect Allow with ec2:RunInstances, ec2:CreateNetworkInterface and ec2:DescribeSubnets: other accounts act on the owner's subnet. To see subnets that other accounts share with you: aws ram list-resources --resource-owner OTHER-ACCOUNTS --resource-type ec2:Subnet

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Create a small test VPC with the two book tags. Keep its ID.
steps.expect: No output. VPC_ID now holds the ID of the new VPC.

steps.text: Create one subnet in the test VPC, with the same tags. Default subnets are not shareable, so you make a new one.
steps.expect: No output. SUBNET_ID now holds the ID of the new subnet.

steps.text: Keep the ARN of the subnet. AWS RAM names every resource in a share by its ARN.
steps.expect: No output. SUBNET_ARN now holds the ARN of the subnet.

steps.text: Create a resource share that holds the subnet. Allow only principals in your organization, and add no principal, so that no other account gets access.
steps.command: aws ram create-resource-share --name saa-organizations-t01 --resource-arns $SUBNET_ARN --no-allow-external-principals --tags key=book,value=saa key=task,value=organizations-t01
steps.expect: No output. SHARE_ARN now holds the ARN of the new resource share.

steps.text: List the resources in the share. Compare the ARN with the subnet you created. If the list is empty, wait a few seconds and run it again.
steps.expect: One row: the ARN of your subnet, with your account ID and your Region in it, and the type ec2:Subnet. The share points to your subnet. It holds no copy.

steps.text: Read which managed permission AWS RAM attached for the subnet type. You did not choose one.
steps.expect: One row: arn:aws:ram::aws:permission/AWSRAMDefaultPermissionSubnet and ec2:Subnet. AWS RAM attached the default permission of the type.

steps.text: Read the actions that this permission allows. AWS RAM turns them into a resource-based policy on the subnet itself.
steps.expect: A JSON text with Effect Allow and the actions ec2:RunInstances, ec2:CreateNetworkInterface and ec2:DescribeSubnets. Another account would launch instances into your subnet, not into a copy.

cleanup.text: Delete the resource share. This stops the sharing. It does not delete the subnet.
Delete the subnet. If the delete fails, wait one minute and run it again.

verify.command: aws ram get-resource-shares --resource-owner SELF --resource-share-status ACTIVE --tag-filters tagKey=task,tagValues=organizations-t01 --query "resourceShares[].resourceShareArn"
verify.expect: An empty list: no active share of this task is left. The VPC check in the next list also returns an empty list.

still_costs: Nothing: there are no additional charges for the VPC itself, and AWS RAM has no additional cost. Delete everything anyway.
Check that the VPC is gone too: aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=tag:task,Values=organizations-t01 --query "Vpcs[].VpcId" must return an empty list.

If the CloudShell session ended before the cleanup, the variables are empty. Find the IDs again with aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=tag:task,Values=organizations-t01 and aws ram get-resource-shares --resource-owner SELF --name saa-organizations-t01.

items.title: Find the management account of your organization
items.kills: "An SCP attached to the organization root limits every account, the management account too."
items.read_only_alternative: This task is read-only. It needs no alternative.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Ask AWS STS which account signs your commands.
Read the organization that your account belongs to: its ID, the ID of its management account and its feature set. Any account in the organization can read this.
steps.expect: An ID that starts with o-, the ID of the management account, and ALL or CONSOLIDATED_BILLING. If AWS answers that your account is not in an organization, stop here: SCPs affect only member accounts, and yours is in no organization.

steps.text: Compare the two IDs. Equal: the management account, where SCPs limit no user or role. Different: a member account, where SCPs can limit you if the feature set is ALL and SCPs are enabled on the root.
steps.expect: Equal or different. Note which case is yours before you read about SCPs.
